query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the degree of lattice matching at the alloy/oxide interface. Specifically, when the alloy composition (especially with the inclusion of Al) promotes the formation of a sub-stoichiometric, coherently bonded oxide—such as an alumina-rich or chromium-rich phase—the interfacial stresses are minimized, leading to a steady, controlled oxide growth that resists cracking and spallation. In contrast, variants with Si or Mn, which do not facilitate the same lattice compatibility, will tend to form less coherent oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (where X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution condition, in the as-cast or heat-treated state with no pre-formed oxides.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to in situ thermal treatment using controlled heating above 900 °C both in oxidative (or corrosive) atmospheres and for comparison under vacuum conditions.
generation.conditions: Temperatures above 900 °C (up to ~1100 °C), extended exposure times (e.g., 10+ hours) in defined oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; comparative treatment under vacuum to isolate oxidation-driven changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial lattice coherence between the growing oxide layer and the underlying HEA substrate, especially as influenced by the formation of Al-rich (or Cr-rich) oxide phases.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, controlled diffusion of reactive elements (notably Al, when present) leads to the formation of an oxide phase that closely matches the lattice parameters of the HEA substrate, thereby reducing thermal stresses and preventing crack initiation. The comparative CALPHAD modeling and in situ HTXRD help predict the oxidation kinetics and phase stability. Without sufficient lattice matching (as may occur in alloys with higher Si or Mn contents), the oxide forms more rapidly, generating stresses that induce cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an optimal amount of Al (or a favorable balance of reactive elements for lattice matching) will develop a slow-growing, coherent oxide layer that remains intact over prolonged high-temperature exposures. In contrast, alloys dominated by Si or Mn will show faster oxide growth rates with increased residual stresses leading to oxide cracking or spallation.
generation.baseline: A controlled reference experiment using the same alloy system treated under vacuum conditions (minimizing oxidation) and comparative in situ HTXRD analysis to distinguish between purely thermal/mechanical and oxidation-driven effects.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEAs in the temperature range of 900–1100 °C with oxidation exposure lasting at least 10 hours; it is relevant to surface phenomena observed in oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres, whereas vacuum conditions serve as the baseline for isolating oxidation effects.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative thresholds for the required elemental balance (especially the roles of Si vs. Mn versus Al) for achieving optimal lattice coherence and the exact stress levels that precipitate cracking remain uncertain. Additionally, the subtle interplay between oxidation kinetics and mechanical stress development needs further quantitative resolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct an in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) study coupled with controlled thermal cycling of CrFeCoNiX alloys (systematically varying X among Si, Mn, and Al) under defined oxidative/corrosive atmospheres versus vacuum. Complement with real-time imaging (e.g., high-resolution SEM or TEM) to monitor the evolution of the oxide layer morphology and stress mapping techniques to evaluate interfacial stresses.
measurements: Phase identification and evolution of oxide layers via HTXRD
Quantitative mass gain measurements to assess oxidation kinetics
Microstructural imaging of the oxide-alloy interface (e.g., using SEM/TEM)
Residual stress mapping at the interface (e.g., via strain measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments reveal that variations in the X element do not lead to differential oxide layer coherence—i.e., if all compositions exhibit either uniformly stable oxide layers or uniformly unstable (cracked/spalled) oxides regardless of their composition—then the hypothesis linking lattice coherence mediated by specific elemental additions (such as Al) to oxide layer stability is falsified.
